name: Ferrith Scar
geological_features: Exposed heavy-metal ore veins running across canyon walls like dark arteries
Impact-shattered highland plateaus rich in metallic deposits
Deep strip-mining canyons carved by previous extraction operations
specific_features: The Scar — a 3,000-km gouge in the northern hemisphere left by an ancient asteroid impact that exposed deep-mantle metals
Magnetic anomaly zones where concentrated iron deposits distort navigation equipment
Abandoned automated mining complexes from a previous colonial era, partially buried in regolith
description: Ferrith Scar is a dense, metal-rich rocky world whose unusually high iron content gives it a gravity that belies its medium frame. The surface is a stark landscape of rust-colored plateaus and deep canyons where heavy-metal ore veins lie exposed to vacuum, glittering darkly in unfiltered starlight. The planet's thin atmosphere offers no protection from radiation or micrometeorite bombardment, leaving the terrain pockmarked and scoured.

There is a brutal beauty to Ferrith Scar — the way the ore veins trace black and silver lines across canyon walls hundreds of meters high, the way the magnetic anomaly zones make compass needles spin and electronics stutter. The silence is absolute except for the creak of thermal expansion in rock faces as the terminator line passes, and the occasional distant rumble of a cliff face calving into a canyon below.

The great Scar that gives the planet its name was carved by an asteroid impact millions of years ago, an event that fractured the northern crust so deeply that mantle-layer metals were thrust to the surface across an area the size of a small continent. A previous colonial power attempted large-scale extraction here, leaving behind the rusting husks of automated mining complexes that still dot the landscape like the bones of dead giants.

Today, prospectors and corporate scouts circle Ferrith Scar with renewed interest as platinum and uranium prices climb across the sector. The abandoned infrastructure could be refurbished at a fraction of the cost of new construction, but the magnetic anomaly zones have claimed several survey ships, and there are persistent rumors that the previous operators left more than just mining equipment behind when they departed.
